newsitem.title: USA: Metal Recovery starts-up de-zincing plant.
newsitem.headline: Metal Recovery starts-up de-zincing plant.

text.p: Metal Recovery Technologies Inc will start-up on Tuesday its first commercial plant to remove zinc from galvanized steel scrap, a move which will change the scrap industry and provide a cheap source of zinc, the company suggested.

Metal Recovery's plant, the first of its kind in the United States, is located in the heart of the Midwest steelbelt. It will clean 75,000 short tons of galvanized steel scrap a year, and produce 3,000 short tons of zinc at less than half the usual cost, the company said.

"Over the next three years we can get to one million tons of scrap which would bring in 35,000 tons of zinc - and that's a small percentage of the available market," Bill Morgan, who devised the process, told Reuters.
Successful pilot tests were completed with the help of Argonne National Laboratory, part of the U.S. Dept of Energy, the American Iron and Steel Institute, General Motors and LTV Corp., Morgan said.
The pilot and commercial plants cost a total $10 million.
The scrap is washed in two consecutive revolving drums containing sodium hydroxide solution which dissolves the zinc.
An electrowinning process removes the zinc from the solution.

Since the early 1980s galvanized sheet steel has been used extensively in making car bodies and some 25 percent ends up as virgin or prompt scrap after the bodies have been stamped. In two to three years time, the first generation of galvanized bodied cars reach the end of the road, ready for recycling.
Morgan estimated that 15 million cars a year are produced, each containing 30 pounds of zinc.
When untreated scrap is remelted by mini-mills in electric furnaces, the zinc escapes as dust which has to be collected.
The dust is converted into zinc metal by some companies such as Horsehead Industries Inc, or encased in a concrete-type material and landfilled by EnviroSource Inc.
But the integrated blast-furnace steel mills need zinc-free scrap which is difficult to obtain, Morgan said. "And the integrated mills are tending to use more scrap."
Metal Recovery aims to built plants near integrated mills and automobile makers to recycle galvanized steel scrap on a tolling basis, creating a closed loop recycling system.

Some scrap yards could face being locked out of a large chunk of the market, Morgan conceded. Horsehead and EnviroSource may also see a shrinking market for zinc dust from mini-mills if more and more galvanized steel scrap is de-zinced and consumed by integrated mills.

A $25 per ton premium on the price galvanized steel scrap would be obtained for dense cleaned shredded scrap, Morgan said. Processing the scrap will cost about $18 to $20 per ton. The cost of producing zinc metal powder or slab will be $450 per short ton at most.
"We are putting in a furnace to melt the zinc metal powder to cast slabs," Morgan said. "Ideally we aim for special high grade metal." LME registration would probably be applied for.
Morgan said that each year two million short tons of virgin galvanized steel scrap and six million tons of old scrap are generated in the United States.
This volume is set to grow domestically and worldwide as more and more of the early cars to use galvanized bodies are scrapped.
The East Chicago plant could process over 200,000 tons of scrap annually if two additional eight-hour shifts were added.
Toyota in Japan also de-zincs scrap but "their different process costs twice as high as ours," Morgan said.
Metal Recovery will show on its Web page how the start-up progressed.

The company signed an agreement with the University of California at Berkley to develop new technology for electrowinning zinc from a caustic solution, thereby cutting power costs compared to energy-intensive conventional process.
-- Huw Jones, New York Commodities 212-859-1646
